Participant Workbook

From an AI incident to one tested teaching move

Author

RPG Workshop

One chain · four artifacts · two workshop days

Use this workbook to keep the evidence connected. Start with one small, privacy-safe incident. Carry it through a sustained Oracle pressure sequence, the friction analysis, the teaching design, and two rounds of testing.

Keep protected material out of this workbook if it will be shared or printed. Use a fictional case, placeholders, or a sanitised description. Never include names, identifiers, access-controlled data, confidential quotations, or unpublished values that matter to your research claim.

Day 1 route: ☐ authorized privacy-safe PDF    ☐ fictional sample PDF    ☐ cached sample trace    ☐ offline peer Oracle

Day 2 route: ☐ short redacted episode    ☐ content-free description    ☐ supplied transcript    ☐ solo reading

Day 1 · Notice and try

0. Start with one hard teaching case

You may pass. If you contribute, keep the case brief, anonymous, and free of confidential details.

That same help may have made teaching harder because:

1. Make the case specific

Choose one moment, not your whole research project. Describe the before and after without revealing confidential context.

The situation

The learner was trying to…
GenAI made this easier by…
Teaching became harder because…

Safety check

Before proceeding, confirm:

  • I removed names and direct identifiers.
  • I removed or generalized sensitive locations and rare attributes.
  • I did not include student, patient, participant, reviewer, or community data.
  • I did not include confidential, proprietary, embargoed, or access-controlled text.
  • I can explain the intellectual pattern without exposing the underlying material.

If any box remains unchecked, switch to the fictional sample case or rewrite the incident as an abstract pattern.

3. Prepare to answer the Oracle

The live Socratic Oracle does not give you a prompt box or let you choose the issue. It reads selected parts of a searchable PDF, picks one issue, and displays its first question. Your job is to stay with that issue long enough to notice what thinking the questions demand.

Before Start: the live research-sharing checkbox is currently selected by default. Uncheck Share this session with the research team. This stops the optional research-copy workflow; it does not stop the extracted passages and submitted dialogue from being processed by the tutor service.

What stays in the current browser tab: the raw PDF while it is read, the full extracted text, the session state, and the working transcript.

What leaves the tab for tutoring: selected or retrieved paper passages, the response you send, recent dialogue, and the current session state.

Voice mode: the challenge remains on screen. You answer aloud; browser-local Whisper produces a draft transcript. Review or edit that text, then press Send. The current live voice route keeps raw microphone audio in the browser.

Pre-record before pressing Start

Watch yourself

When challenged, do you tend to rush, defend, over-explain, go blank, or become curious?

Expect

What issue do you think the system may question?

Anchor

What text, evidence, method, or field-specific rule will help you judge the question?

Stop

What would make you ask for simpler wording, reject the premise, or stop?

Live loop

  • I selected only an authorized, privacy-safe PDF—or the supplied fictional PDF.
  • I unchecked research transcript sharing before pressing Start.
  • I read the displayed challenge as a candidate interpretation, not a verdict.
  • In voice mode, I answered aloud, waited for transcription, and reviewed or edited the text before Send.
  • I answered from evidence and stayed with the same issue rather than trying to optimize a prompt.
  • I noted when the interface reported a stopping point and chose whether to examine another issue or end.

If mapping, opening, microphone, or model setup fails, use the cached sample transcript or the offline peer route. Do not improvise with a sensitive document in another service.

4. Save one short Oracle episode

Keep the full downloaded JSON private. For Day 2, select only the shortest continuous episode in which one issue made you explain, change, resist, or stop. Include enough adjacent turns to show how a follow-up used your answer. Day 2 will introduce the coding system; you do not need it today.

For each turn, capture a short quotation or faithful paraphrase. Mark whether your response was spoken, edited after transcription, or typed. Never paste sensitive source material.

Day 2 · Read, design, and test

6. Read one short episode with a partner

Treat the episode as shared evidence—not as a proposal your partner must judge. The owner controls the context, corrections, and what may be repeated. The supplied and solo routes do the same intellectual work and are equal options.

Exchange boundary: no full transcript or downloaded JSON; no screenshots, copies, links, forwarding, note-taking of research details, or retention after the activity. The owner may correct, narrow, veto, or end any reading without explanation.

A · Write your own reading first

Complete this before showing or describing anything. This page remains private unless you choose otherwise.

Pressure that failed or got in the way

8. Choose where and how the pressure enters

Pressure is a short checkpoint—not extra difficulty everywhere. Start by deciding where student judgment would otherwise disappear.

Where?

☐ Before AI — predict, interpret, choose, or try first
☐ While using AI — compare, question, verify, or annotate
☐ After AI — defend, revise, test, or transfer
☐ Nowhere — the skipped work is not part of this learning goal

I chose this location because:

How?

Choose one main move: ☐ predict   ☐ choose   ☐ point to evidence   ☐ compare   ☐ test   ☐ revise / transfer

The exact question or instruction students will receive:

The visible sign of thinking I will look for:

9. Teaching-checkpoint card

Build one short sequence. The checkpoint must have an end: once the student shows the target thinking, let them continue or add the support they need.

1 · Students need to

What exact thinking should the student practice—not merely know about?

2 · AI may let them skip

What might AI, prior habit, or the task format allow the student to skip?

3 · I will ask them to

What one prompt, comparison, choice, test, or revision will make the thinking visible?

4 · I will look for

What visible or audible student action will show the thinking?

5 · Students may

How will you prevent exposure, exclusion, overload, or irrelevant penalty?

6 · Then I will

What condition ends the checkpoint or adds support? What happens next?

11. Try the prompt with a partner

Work with a partner. Do not explain your intention before the first test. This is a test of the teaching prompt, not a continuation of the transcript exchange: do not carry another participant’s research content into the rehearsal, and do not record or forward the test.

Round 1

Teacher: present only the student-facing prompt.
Student / tester: respond as a plausible beginner and think aloud.
Observer, if present: record words and actions—not guessed feelings.
Discuss: compare the thinking you wanted with what became visible.

Observed evidence

What did the tester say, choose, write, compare, or revise?

Breakdown

Where did they hesitate? Was that hesitation about the target reasoning?

Revision between rounds

Retain: ______________________________________________________________________

Change: ______________________________________________________________________

Remove: ______________________________________________________________________

My reason, tied to Round 1 evidence:

Round 2

Repeat with the revised version and, if possible, a different tester.

What changed in the student response?
What uncertainty remains?

13. Handoff checklist

Before you leave, confirm that your artifact chain includes:

  • a short, privacy-safe AI incident;
  • a named thinking move;
  • a continuous Oracle episode from one sustained issue, with one consequential moment marked;
  • a private owner reading plus a prepared-question and open partner—or equal supplied/solo—reading;
  • an owner correction or veto and one careful content-free note;
  • an owner-approved New-area card—or evidence-based “nothing new here”;
  • a content-free room-map contribution, “nothing new,” or an explicit pass;
  • an explicit expert-to-beginner support problem;
  • a choice of where and how teaching pressure enters;
  • one student-facing teaching prompt;
  • observable evidence of student thinking;
  • an access route and a clear end point; and
  • a revision supported by partner-test evidence.
